issues.description: The manuscript presents simulated/randomized data as if they were substantive findings, while noting in multiple places that the abstract, methods, and results are based on dummy Qualtrics-generated data. This makes the reported inferential results uninterpretable as evidence about the phenomenon and creates a fundamental mismatch between the stated goal of reporting a replication and the actual content.
issues.quote: [IMPORTANT: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.description: The methods and results are explicitly described as written from randomized placeholder data, yet the manuscript proceeds to interpret significance tests and theoretical implications. This invalidates all reported statistical conclusions and any replication claims.
issues.quote: [IMPORTANT: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.description: The manuscript indicates that data collection had not yet occurred or that results would be updated later, yet reports full statistical analyses. Without actual collected data, there is no empirical basis for the reported findings.
issues.quote: These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.description: The manuscript claims a 'close to very close replication' despite substantial deviations from the original studies: merging two separate experiments into one, changing from behavioral donation with real money to hypothetical donation, moving from lab to MTurk online, applying intervention to the joint condition, and altering measurement. These are major design changes likely to affect the psychological process under study, making the replication classification overstated.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition...

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames the study as a direct/close replication while the design differs importantly from the target article in participant pool, setting, procedure, incentives, and dependent measure. This overstates comparability and may mislead readers about what a null or divergent effect means.
issues.quote: We therefore embark on a well-powered pre-registered close to very close replication of Small et al. (2007).

issues.description: Participants are said to have selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions rather than being randomly assigned. This destroys experimental control, introduces selection bias, and invalidates causal interpretation of condition differences.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The design is described as within-subject, but all analyses and tables imply independent groups across six between-subject conditions with separate cell sizes summing to N=1000. This contradiction prevents understanding of the actual design and raises questions about the validity of the analyses used.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.description: If the study were truly within-subject, standard between-subject two-way ANOVA with residual df=994 would be inappropriate; repeated-measures or mixed models would be needed. The reported analyses imply between-subject data, contradicting the design description.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.description: The reported cell counts across the six conditions are mutually exclusive and sum to the full sample, which is incompatible with a within-subject design in which each participant contributes to multiple cells. This indicates either the design description or the analysis/reporting is wrong.

The original studies used actual donations from money participants had received; the replication uses an imaginary donation response. This changes the dependent variable from consequential helping behavior to stated intention, which may rely on different motivational processes and weakens construct validity for replicating the original donation effect.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: Combining Studies 1 and 3 into one experiment changes the operationalization of explicit versus implicit deliberation and may alter how participants construe the task. This risks testing a different construct from the original separate experiments.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect

issues.description: Applying the explicit intervention to the joint condition adds a manipulation not present in the target Study 3, changing the meaning of the joint condition and undermining correspondence with the original implicit manipulation.
issues.quote: The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.description: Because participants reportedly selected their preferred conditions, any observed differences could reflect preexisting preferences or characteristics rather than effects of identifiability or intervention. Causal claims about debiasing are therefore unwarranted.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The manuscript does not provide a coherent account of assignment to conditions. It first implies an experimental design but then states participants selected conditions. Details of allocation procedure, implementation, and whether assignment was randomized are missing.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: Critical procedural details are omitted from the main text: the wording of the intervention, stimuli shown in each condition, timing, attention check content, exclusion criteria thresholds, and the exact questionnaire items. Reliance on external links without a sufficient in-text summary hampers evaluation and replication.
issues.quote: For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below

issues.description: Although the study is called pre-registered, the manuscript does not specify the date of registration relative to data collection, the exact preregistered hypotheses/analyses, or deviations from preregistration in a transparent tabular form. Given the major design changes and placeholder analyses, researcher degrees of freedom remain unclear.
issues.quote: Gilad supervised each step in the project, conducted the pre-registrations, and ran data collection.

issues.description: The manuscript states data collection was launched at the start of the study period but provides limited detail about what was preregistered and when. This raises concerns about whether the analysis plan was finalized before data collection and whether decisions were influenced by observed data.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period.

issues.description: The manuscript contains unresolved placeholders for key materials, such as cloud folder links for presentation and peer reviews. This signals incompleteness and limits transparency.
issues.quote:
Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here>
Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>

issues.description: The manuscript claims the sample size was determined by power analysis, but no target effect, alpha, desired power, design assumptions, or resulting required N are reported in the main text. This prevents assessment of whether the study is adequately powered, especially for interactions and subgroup comparisons.
issues.quote: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary

issues.description: The reported sample characteristics for the Qualtrics-generated responses are implausible for an MTurk replication of this topic (mean age 67.8, age range 18-120). Even if dummy data, these values are then used in the manuscript's tables and can mislead about the intended sampling frame and comparability to the original sample.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.description: The target study used university participants in a campus setting, whereas the replication plans to use MTurk workers online. This shift may alter responsiveness to victim-identifiability manipulations and donation choices, but the implications for generalizability and comparability are not adequately discussed.
issues.quote: Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.description: The text reports means for the identifiable and statistical conditions that do not match the descriptive statistics in Table 7. Based on Table 7, the collapsed means are approximately 2.54 for identifiable and 2.23 for statistical, but the text reverses and alters them. This undermines confidence in the analysis and interpretation.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.description: The narrative interpretation of the main identifiability effect is inconsistent with Table 7, where identifiable condition means are 2.58 and 2.50 and statistical condition means are 2.46 and 2.01. The reported text appears to swap labels and use values not derivable from the table as stated.
issues.quote:
Table 7
...
Identifiable victim condition ... 2.58 ... 2.50 ...
Statistical victim condition ... 2.46 ... 2.01 ...
...
participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.description: In Table 10, the Identifiable vs Statistical comparison has t = -2.40 but d = 0.076, implying an opposite sign convention or reporting error. Effect size sign should correspond to the direction of the contrast as defined. Such inconsistencies suggest computational or reporting mistakes.

Several pairwise comparisons are reported as statistically significant while the confidence intervals for Cohen's d include zero, which is inconsistent if the CI pertains to the same tested effect. Either the CIs are miscomputed, are for a different quantity, or the p-values are wrong.
issues.quote:
Identifiable VS Statistical | ... d | 0.076 | [-0.05, 0.20] | .049*
Statistical VS Joint | ... d | 0.08 | [-0.07, 0.23] | .041*

issues.description: The manuscript interprets a Bonferroni-adjusted post-hoc pairwise comparison for perceived impact despite only a marginal omnibus effect (p = .045) and confidence intervals including zero. Given the placeholder data and inconsistent CI reporting, this is not trustworthy; moreover, the stated extension hypothesis predicts identifiable > statistical, but the only significant pair is statistical > joint.

The extension hypothesis predicts identifiable victims should elicit higher perceived donation impact than statistical victims. However, the only reported significant difference is between statistical and joint conditions, and the identifiable vs statistical comparison is nonsignificant. The discussion sentence in the abstract claiming support is therefore inaccurate.
issues.quote:
It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims.
...
Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: The abstract states support for the perceived-impact hypothesis, but the detailed results do not support the preregistered direction (identifiable > statistical). This is a clear mismatch between abstract and results.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: The theoretical rationale for perceived impact is inconsistent. One section argues identifiable victims should produce higher perceived impact because aid is easier to picture and rescue proportion is 100%; the reported abstract claim instead frames lower perceived impact for identifiable/joint conditions as support. This indicates conceptual confusion about the expected direction of the construct.
issues.quote:
It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims.
...
Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim

issues.description: The planned and reported contrast compares the identifiable/no-intervention cell to a combination of all other cells, but no details are given on how this was implemented. Depending on coding, such a comparison in a factorial ANOVA with unbalanced cells may not correspond to a standard preplanned contrast, and the manuscript instead reports it as a t-test without justification. This is especially problematic because the original contrast involved four conditions, whereas the replication includes six and altered design structure.
issues.quote: we also conducted a t-test to study if the mean of identifiable/no intervention condition is different from the mean of combining other five conditions on donation.

issues.description: The manuscript does not explain whether post-hoc tests were pooled-error contrasts from ANOVA, independent-samples t tests, or estimated marginal mean comparisons, nor how multiplicity was handled across the many tests. This impedes reproducibility and evaluation of error rates.
issues.quote: Post-hoc contrast test (Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant)

issues.description: Donation is bounded from $0 to $5 and likely discrete/ordinal in unit increments, yet the manuscript drops the original ordered probit approach and uses ANOVA/t-tests without justification or robustness checks. Given potential non-normality and heteroscedasticity for bounded donation data, assumptions should be addressed.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression ... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.description: No information is given about checking ANOVA assumptions such as normality, homogeneity of variance, independence, or handling of bounded/discrete outcomes. This is particularly important given the donation variable and the potential mismatch between stated within-subject design and between-subject analyses.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA

issues.description: The manuscript states that participants with prior knowledge and attention-check failures were excluded, but does not report how many were excluded for each reason, from what initial sample, or by condition. Without a participant flow and condition-specific exclusions, selection effects and attrition bias cannot be assessed.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: There is no description of item nonresponse, partial completions, or any missing data handling strategy for donation or feeling measures. This limits confidence in the analyses and reproducibility.
issues.quote: All measures and manipulations conducted for this investigation are reported

issues.description: The content, placement, and scoring rule for the attention check are not provided. Because exclusions are based on it, this omission matters for reproducibility and interpretation.
issues.quote: those who failed the attention check

issues.description: The manuscript analyzes an 'aggregated feelings' variable but does not define how it was computed, whether items were averaged or summed, whether any reverse coding was used, and whether internal consistency was acceptable. Without this information, the validity of the aggregate is unclear.
issues.quote: segregated affective reactions which were combined to form an aggregated feeling in the previous statistical tests

issues.description: No response scale anchors, number of points, or psychometric properties are reported for the affective feeling items or perceived impact measure. This prevents evaluation of measurement quality and comparability with the original study.
issues.quote: These items included beliefs about the severity of the crisis, the perceived trustworthiness of the charity, the expected accountability of funds, evaluation of organizational efficiency, and the appropriateness of donation to help the victims.

issues.description: The perceived impact extension is theoretically central but its exact item wording and relation to the original feeling measures are not specified. It is unclear whether this is a validated measure, a single item, or adapted wording, limiting interpretability.
issues.quote: We aim to extend the replication study by considering the “perceived impact of donation” as one of the feeling variables

issues.description: The manuscript describes correlations as showing whether affective feelings 'predict' donation. Correlation within conditions does not establish prediction in a causal or temporal sense, especially with simultaneous self-report measures.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.description: The manuscript calls the identifiable victim effect 'crucial' for encouraging altruistic behavior despite citing a meta-analytic mean effect size of only 0.05. This overstates the empirical strength of the phenomenon and underplays the possibility that effects are small and context-dependent.
issues.quote: Although the overall mean effect size was only 0.05, the significance of the identifiable victim effect is still crucial to encourage altruistic behaviour towards the needy

issues.description: The manuscript refers to 'Table 7 summarizes the current replication' before later labeling a different Table 7 as descriptive statistics for donation. Inconsistent numbering hinders interpretation and suggests the manuscript is not finalized.
issues.quote:
Figure 2 specifies the classification of the replications ... Table 7 summarizes the current replication as a "close to very close replication".
...
Table 7

Descriptive statistics for donation across conditions

issues.description: Table 4 appears to contain duplicated replication columns/entries and malformed formatting, making it unclear what values correspond to what source. This undermines confidence in basic reporting accuracy.
issues.quote:
| Original study | Qualtrics generated response
Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.description: The manuscript reports derived effect sizes and confidence intervals for the original study from supplementary calculations, but does not explain the formulas, assumptions, or whether these were based on exact cell ns and SDs. Reconstruction from incomplete published information can be error-prone and should be documented.
issues.quote: The effect size of the identifiable victim effect was not reported in the original study. Further calculation of the effect size and confidence interval was included in the supplementary

issues.description: The manuscript presents the availability heuristic as if it directly explains responses to personalized victims, but the original literature more commonly frames this in terms of affect, imagery, identifiability, or evaluability. The conceptual bridge is underdeveloped and risks conflating distinct mechanisms.
issues.quote: The “availability heuristic” (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973)... is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual

issues.description: There is no statement about ethics/IRB approval or informed consent procedures, despite using human participants and charitable donation scenarios. This is a basic reporting requirement.
issues.quote: Method

issues.description: Participant compensation for the planned MTurk sample is not specified, even though incentives can affect donation responses and sample quality. This also limits comparability to the original study, which provided $5.
issues.quote: Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified

issues.description: The replication updates victim information from the Save the Children website because the original materials were dated. While understandable, this changes the contextual content and potentially the emotional potency of stimuli, which may limit direct comparability.
issues.quote: We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.

issues.description: Hypothesis 5 is split into 5a and 5b in the table but referred to as singular in the text, and the formatting conflates multiple predictions into single cells. This makes it unclear which tests correspond to which preregistered hypotheses.
issues.quote: 5a   5b | An identifiable victim elicits more affective feelings than an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics and statistical victims  Learning about the identifiable victim effect elicits less affective feelings...

issues.description: The manuscript conducts many ANOVAs, post-hoc tests, and condition-specific correlations across multiple outcomes. Bonferroni is mentioned for some pairwise comparisons, but there is no coherent familywise or false-discovery control strategy across the full set of hypotheses and exploratory tests, increasing the chance of false positives.
issues.quote: Table 9 to 18 summarise statistical testings for the hypotheses of this replication.

issues.description: The text says Tables 9 to 18 summarize the statistical tests, but only Tables 9 to 15 are presented in the manuscript excerpt. Missing tables impede full review of the analyses.
issues.quote: Table 9 to 18 summarise statistical testings for the hypotheses of this replication.

issues.description: The manuscript reports 95% CIs for partial eta squared but does not specify how they were computed. Some intervals are extremely narrow and begin at zero, which may reflect software defaults or imprecision. Without method details, readers cannot verify these values.
